title: We Assumed an Indian Privacy Law Didn’t Apply to a US App.

Dpdp Act Data Privacy Mobile App Development Startup Product Strategy We Assumed an Indian Privacy Law Didn’t Apply to a US App. A Partner’s Questionnaire Proved Us Wrong. GMTA Software Solutions Pvt Ltd 5 min read · Oct 26, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Dana Whitfield’s first reaction to the questionnaire was relief that it wasn’t hers to answer. Stride, the fitness-coaching app she ran engineering for, was a Delaware company with a Delaware cloud account and a US legal team. A telecom distribution partner in India wanted to bundle Stride into a subscriber plan, and its procurement team had sent over a vendor questionnaire with a section headed “DPDP readiness.” Dana forwarded it to legal with a one-line note: This is India’s law; we’re a US company, can you confirm we can answer not applicable? Legal came back two days later with a different answer. The Act reaches processing that happens outside India when it is connected to offering goods or services to people in India. Stride had about 48,000 monthly active users there, an Indian pricing tier, and a rupee payment option. It was in scope, and nobody at the company had noticed because nothing in the product, the roadmap, or the vendor list had ever been labeled “India.” The investigation Dana did what she should have done a year earlier: she mapped where personal data actually lived. She expected a handful of systems. The map came out at fourteen. The primary database was the one everyone thought about. Around it sat an analytics warehouse, a support CRM, an email platform, three third-party SDKs in the mobile app, a crash reporter, a session-replay tool, and the logs from Stride’s AI coaching chat, which stored every prompt and response for quality review. Then she ran the test that mattered. She picked a test account and tried to erase it end to end. The primary database cleared in an hour. The analytics warehouse, the CRM, the replay tool, and the chat logs kept their copies. There was no single place that knew they existed. What the map and the test showed: 14 systems held personal data, and the team had been tracking 5 of them 0 of the 14 had a documented deletion path that ran from a user request 1 bundled consent checkbox at signup, with no record of which version of the notice a user had accepted 0 breach runbooks, and no named owner for writing the notice to affected users Then she read what the framework required. The Rules were notified in November 2025 with an 18-month phase-in, which meant most obligations would apply around May 13, 2027. They called for a separate, plain-language notice stating a specific purpose, and for access, correction, update and erasure requests to be answered within 90 days. The penalty ceiling for failing to keep reasonable security safeguards was ₹250 crore. IBM’s 2026 research put the average data breach in India at ₹25.5 crore, up almost 16% in a year. The ceiling was not a prediction. It was still nearly ten times what the average breach already cost. Founder takeaway: The question to ask is never “does this law apply to us?” in the abstract. It’s “where is our users’ data, and could we find it, delete it, and explain it on a deadline?” Stride couldn’t answer that for a single account, and the gap had nothing to do with which country the company was in. The rebuild Dana didn’t try to ship everything at once. She split the work into the two flows users would actually see and the three layers underneath them. The first release was consent and notice: separate, purpose-level consent records, versioned notices, and a withdrawal control that was as easy to reach as the original opt-in. The second was a rights-request flow with identity checks and a timer, wired so a deletion request fanned out to every system on the map, including the AI chat logs. Underneath those, the team added retention schedules and automated deletion, audit logging with named owners for each safeguard, and a breach runbook with notification templates. She also commissioned a penetration test, partly because IBM’s India data found offensive security testing cut average breach costs by ₹2.47 crore, the largest saving of any measure it studied, and partly because a tested control is far easier to defend than an assumed one. Stride’s engineers reviewed the AI features too, since prompt logs, embeddings and evaluation sets were all copies of personal data the original map had missed. Her team found the architecture principles in GMTA’s guide to privacy-first design for AI applications a useful checklist for that review. What actually changed 14 of 14 systems mapped, each with a named owner, by the end of month one 0 → 6 days average end-to-end erasure time, measured in month two, with a target of 30 days 100% of new Indian sign-ups captured with purpose-level, versioned consent by month two, and 71% of existing Indian users re-consented by month three 3 days → 5 hours to produce a plain-language breach notice in a tabletop exercise, between the first and third runs 1 distribution partnership signed, after Stride returned the questionnaire with evidence instead of a “not applicable” The telecom partner’s procurement team told Dana the readiness section had decided it among the three shortlisted vendors. Stride sent screenshots of the consent flow, the request portal and the tabletop results. The other two sent policy documents.
